stem: According to Wovoka's message, what would the dance bring about?

stimulus.source_note: Wovoka's message ('The Messiah Letter'), obtained by ethnologist James Mooney from a Cheyenne delegate in 1891 and published in Mooney, The Ghost-Dance Religion and the Sioux Outbreak of 1890 (1896). Public domain. Text verified against the Digital History (University of Houston) transcription of Mooney's report.
stimulus.text:
Wovoka, the Northern Paiute prophet, 'The Messiah Letter,' as recorded by ethnologist James Mooney, 1891 (ellipses mark omissions):

"When you get home you must make a dance to continue five days. Dance four successive nights, and the last night keep up the dance until the morning of the fifth day, when all must bathe in the river and then disperse to their homes. ... The dead are still alive again. ... When the time comes there will be no more sickness and everyone will be young again. Do not refuse to work for the whites and do not make any trouble with them until you leave them. ... I want you to dance every six weeks."

options.text: A great war that would drive the army from the Plains
options.misconception: Background: Wovoka told his followers not to fight and not to make trouble with whites.

options.text: A new treaty giving the Lakota the Black Hills
options.misconception: Background: the message promises a renewed world, not a treaty; the Black Hills had been taken after gold was found there in 1874.

options.text: Schools where Native children would learn English
options.misconception: Background: English-language schooling was Pratt's program at Carlisle, not Wovoka's promise.

options.text: The return of the dead, the buffalo, and a renewed world

rationales.A: Background: Wovoka told his followers not to fight and not to make trouble with whites.
rationales.B: Background: the message promises a renewed world, not a treaty. The Black Hills had been taken after gold was found there in 1874.
rationales.C: Background: English-language schooling was Pratt's program at Carlisle, not Wovoka's promise.
rationales.D: Wovoka promises 'the dead are still alive again' and a dance that renews the world. The hope is spiritual renewal, not a battle or a treaty.
rationales.general:
Picture a circle of dancers holding hands, singing through the night until morning.
1. Read what the dance is for. Five days of dancing, then bathing in the river and going home.
2. Read what it promises. The dead alive again, sickness gone, everyone young again.
3. Name the hope. A world made new, not a war won.
Remember: a religion of renewal promises a new world, not a new battle.
